transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, Dr. [Name]. Um, the main reason I came in is that I just get pulled off track so easily. Like, I'll be trying to finish up a project for school, maybe working on a dashboard or something, and then... I don't know, one Slack ping goes off, or I hear a song lyric, or I just get a random idea for a totally different project. And suddenly, I've completely lost the thread of what I was supposed to be doing. It just keeps happening.
When you get pulled off track like this, do you also feel restless or like you have a lot of energy that's hard to contain, or is it more just that your attention shifts to the new thing?

Um, it's kind of both, actually. My attention definitely shifts to the new thing, but I do get that restless feeling too. Like, if I have to sit still through a long Zoom call for a class, or just quietly work in one place for a while, I start feeling this... uncomfortable pressure in my body. It just feels like I need to get up and pace around, or at least be doing something with my hands.

How long have you been experiencing these difficulties with attention and restlessness? Can you think back to when they first started—was this something you noticed in elementary school, or is this more recent?

Um, it's been going on for a really long time. Definitely since elementary school. I remember my teachers would always write comments on my report cards about me rushing through worksheets and losing track of directions. And, um, talking over my classmates during group work was a pretty common one, too. 

At home, it was kind of the same. My parents actually used to have to sit right beside me while I did my homework. If they didn't, I would just wander off or start doing something else entirely before I even finished what I was working on. So, yeah, it's definitely not a new thing.

You mentioned these difficulties started in elementary school. Before you turned 12 years old, were you experiencing these attention and restlessness problems in more than just school—like at home, with friends, or in other activities as well?

Yeah, definitely. It wasn't just at school. Like I said, my parents had to sit with me at home to get me to do my homework, or I'd just wander off. And even with other things, like chores or just getting ready in the morning, they were always having to remind me what I was supposed to be doing. I'd start cleaning my room and then find a toy and just start playing with it instead. 

And with friends... I think I just had a lot of energy. I was always the one who wanted to run around and play games, and I had a hard time sitting still if we were supposed to be watching a movie or something. So yeah, it was pretty much everywhere, not just in the classroom.

Looking back at your childhood, would you say these attention and restlessness problems were causing real problems for you—like affecting your grades, your relationships with other kids, or getting you into trouble at home or school?

Yeah, it definitely caused problems back then, and... well, it still does now. Like, I've actually lost a few small freelance contracts recently, and I even missed out on this big portfolio competition because I just... I couldn't get my act together to follow through cleanly. People just felt like they couldn't rely on me. And it's frustrating because it affects my relationships, too. Some of my friends and people I collaborate with are kind of hesitant to work with me now. They always say they like my ideas, but... yeah, actually getting the work done with me is a different story.

When you're in situations where you need to wait—like standing in line, or waiting for someone to finish talking before you respond—do you find yourself fidgeting a lot, interrupting people, or blurting things out? Or is it more that you just lose focus on what's happening around you?

It's definitely more on the interrupting side, especially when I'm working with other people. Like, if we're brainstorming or something, I'll just blurt out my idea right in the middle of someone else talking. Or I'll just jump onto our shared Figma board and start adding things before they've even finished explaining what they want to do. I don't mean to be rude, I just get really excited about the idea and it just comes out. But then afterward, I can tell I came off as pushy or like I wasn't listening, which... I guess I wasn't really, because I was just focused on getting my thought out.

You mentioned missing out on portfolio competitions and losing freelance contracts recently. In a typical week right now, how many hours would you say you're actually able to focus productively on a single task before getting distracted or needing to switch to something else?

Hours? Honestly, it's rarely ever hours at a time. It's usually just a few minutes. Like, I can sit down to read a research article or watch a UX tutorial, and... well, after just a couple of minutes, I'll realize my eyes have just been moving across the page or the screen, but I have absolutely no idea what I just took in. I just stop absorbing the information, so I either have to go back and start over or just switch to something else entirely.

When you're not working on a project or trying to focus on something specific, do you find it hard to just relax or sit quietly? Like, do you feel a constant need to be doing something, or do you feel more calm when you're not under pressure to concentrate?

Yeah, it's pretty hard for me to just sit quietly and relax. Even if I try to do something that's supposed to be calming, like reading a book for fun or doing a simple sketching exercise, I can't just be quiet with it. I always end up talking to myself, or I have to put music on, or I'll stop to check something on my phone. Sometimes I even turn a simple, relaxing sketch into this huge, complicated project instead of just letting it be what it was supposed to be. I just can't seem to turn my brain off and just be still.
Have you ever had periods—maybe lasting a few days or longer—where you felt unusually happy or energized, or where you needed much less sleep than normal but still felt great and full of energy?

No, I don't think I've ever had anything like that. I mean, I have times where I'm excited about a new project, like I mentioned, but it's not like I feel unusually energized for days on end or stop needing sleep. My sleep is pretty normal, and I don't get those kinds of extreme highs where I feel like I can just keep going without resting.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient presents with lifelong history of inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity beginning in elementary school, persisting across multiple settings (home, school, work). Core symptoms include: difficulty sustaining attention (loses focus within minutes), easy distractibility, restlessness/fidgeting, difficulty waiting turns, frequent interruptions/blurting, and inability to relax quietly. Symptoms cause significant functional impairment (lost contracts, missed opportunities, damaged relationships). Onset before age 12 confirmed with multiple informants (parents, teachers). No evidence of manic episodes. Presentation is consistent with ADHD, combined presentation (F90.2 would be more specific if hyperactivity-impulsivity and inattention both clearly present in current presentation; however, F90.9 reflects the comprehensive mixed symptomatology and severity).
